subject: bat
pitch: A fruit bat with its wings spread wide. A fluffy golden-brown body, a fox-like face with big dark eyes and a moist black nose, pointed ears, and leathery charcoal wings stretched between long finger bones with a small hooked claw on each thumb. It clutches a half-eaten fig in its feet.
reasoning:
I'm planning the fruit bat's proportions for a TypeScript SDK model—aiming for a realistic flying fox scale with roughly a 1.2 m wingspan and 0.22 m body length, oriented facing +Z and centered at the origin.

I'm weighing whether to pose it flying with wings spread in midair, since the pitch's "wings spread wide" clutching a fig suggests flight rather than a perch, which affects whether it needs to touch the ground or stay elevated.

Settling on: the bat lands with feet at y=0, fig held in its claws, wings flared out and slightly raised like it just touched down—stylized but coherent. Now I'm turning to planning out the actual geometry and coordinates with the SDK, keeping the limb count manageable.

Setting up the skeleton...

I'll simplify and use 3 points with 2 names for the wing spans, skipping the tip joint complexity. Then for fingers, I'm setting up wing membranes stretched between the finger edges and the body edge using the membrane helper.

Positioning the finger joints...

Edges need consistent root-to-tip direction, so each finger chain works fine paired with another finger since both run wrist-to-tip. For membranes against the body, I'll need to represent the body side as a points array running the same direction, maybe tied to the wing joint bone. Planning out the membrane pairs now, starting with finger one connecting to finger two.

For the leading edge membrane I'll pair the arm chain against f1, accepting the mismatched arc lengths between shoulder-to-wrist and wrist-to-tip since the resampling will just stretch the membrane slightly rather than break it. I'll move on and double check the default membrane row settings next.

Now I'm working out the hips and legs — placing the hip joint, then figuring out where the feet land since bats grip fruit with their feet held forward near the body rather than straight down. I'm defining each leg as a two-bone limb (thigh and shin) with a bend direction pushing the knee backward and outward, estimating hip-to-foot distance against the limb lengths to make sure the reach works.

I'm also deciding whether the fig is clutched between both feet in front of the chest or the bat is simply sitting with its rump on the ground and legs raised to hold the fruit — trying to keep the lowest point of the body at y≈0 while the feet stay elevated holding the fig near chest height.

I think I should stop second-guessing the pose details and just commit to coordinates: hips at [0, 0.2, -0.02] with the body tilted so the belly/rump sits near ground level, feet positioned to clutch the fig in front at chest height, and I'll verify the leg lengths work out geometrically before writing the actual code.

That puts the rump's bottom at roughly y=0.015, which is within the acceptable sink tolerance. Now I'm working out the head joint placement and sweep path from neck to snout, shaping a fox-like tapered skull with radii shrinking from about 0.065 near the crown to 0.025 at the snout tip.

Setting up the spine chain hierarchy...

The sweep ends right at the head joint, covering the neck fine. For the golden-brown fluffy body color, I'll keep it simple with a mottle paint blending gold and brown tones rather than adding fur-tuft cards, which would add too much complexity.

Now I'm nailing down the full color palette: golden-brown body, cream belly for countershading, charcoal wings, dark eyes with white highlights, dark nose, warm inner ears, dark claws, and a purple fig with pink inner flesh and green stem. I'll use the same mottle paint for the head sweep as the body, and need to import countershade, mottle, and spots from the builder library for these effects.

Then I'm working out eye placement on the head joint using local coordinate words like forward, up, and left/right relative to the model's orientation -- positioning the eyes slightly forward and up from the head joint, offset to each side by a small amount, and making them big dark spheres with tiny white highlight spheres for a cute, expressive look.

Working out the angle convention so left side maps to -90 and right to +90 depending on sign s, and settling on roughly -80*s for eye placement to angle them slightly forward rather than straight to the side, placed around t=0.45-0.5 with radius 0.024 for big eyes. Now I'm moving to the ears, planning pointed triangular shapes extruded from an outline and positioned near the back of the head around t=0.2.

Writing ear extrude code...

For wings, I'm planning the membrane color and finger bone rods, then laying out shoulder, elbow, and wrist points per side to build the arm chain with proper parenting to the chest joint.

Fingers branch off the wrist joint, and I'm sketching four finger-tip positions that sweep from a leading edge toward the trailing edge of the wing to define its overall curved shape.

Each finger becomes its own small chain from wrist to tip, aimed so the joint rotation follows the digit direction, using role "digit" with unique names like fingerL1. For the membrane surfaces, I'm pairing a leading-edge path (shoulder-elbow-wrist) against each finger chain so the skin stretches dynamically as the pose changes.

Still defining membrane geometry...

Let me set membrane color using a mottled charcoal paint for that leathery look, and think through wingspan proportions—fruit bat wingspan is around 1.5m, so I'll scale the half-span and tip positions accordingly.

For the thumb claw, I'm working out a small hooked bone structure at the wrist joint, using a swept bezier curve to create the hook shape with a bone-colored rod leading to a pointed claw tip.

Now I'm moving to the legs, setting up hip joints and using a limb function to generate chains of points for the hip, knee, and ankle, naming each joint along the way to build out the leg skeleton structure.

I'm working out the hip-to-foot positioning for the legs, placing the figurine the bat holds in front of its chest, and figuring out limb lengths and bend direction for the single knee joint between hip and foot.

For the fig itself, I'm thinking of a pear-shaped lathe profile with tapered radius points from base to tip, and considering how to render the "half-eaten" look by cutting a bite notch into the shape rather than just a plain lathe.

I'll use a small cylinder disc stuck along the normal as the pink flesh cap at the bite mark, with its axis aligned to the surface normal. For the fig body itself, I'm positioning it between the holding feet with a lathe outline shaped like a pear, tuning the radius points and smoothing to get the right silhouette, then adding a thin green stem rod at the top.

For the eyes, I'm placing spheres along the head sweep at specific angles with slight embedding, then adding tiny white highlight spheres offset slightly outward and upward from each eye's frame to catch the light.

I'm placing the highlight sphere relative to the eye's offset, sinking it halfway in for a natural shine, then working out nose placement near the snout tip using the sweep's radius at that point to size and embed a small sphere.

For the nose geometry I'll flatten a small sphere slightly for a fox-like snout shape. For the coat, I'm thinking countershading with a mottled gold-brown back and cream belly for realism, and considering whether to add fur tuft cards scattered along the spine using an SVG texture for extra fluffiness, though that adds some risk.

For the fur cards I'm working out how the scatter function filters placement by surface normal, and how texture tinting works with a plain colored fill plus a color parameter.

Now I'm working through the skeleton and joint hierarchy for the bat body—spine chain naming, hip and leg joints, wing arm chains with shoulder/elbow/wrist, finger chains for the wing membrane, and how each piece parents to the next. I'm placing coordinates for the ears (checking head joint position and tilting the ear plane backward), the wing membrane edges connecting the arm and finger chains, and tapering sweeps for the arm bones and legs.

I'm also calculating body proportions carefully—checking that the spine sweep's lowest point doesn't sink unrealistically below the floor, adjusting the hip joint height and spine path points accordingly, and verifying that the head, neck, and wing shoulder positions stay consistent with the body radius profile so nothing clips awkwardly.
